paraphrase: First section on the body, the breath (ānāpāna). The Buddha asks how a monk abides contemplating the body in the body. Here a monk, gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting the body upright, and establishing mindfulness in front (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā). Mindful he breathes in; mindful he breathes out. Breathing in long he knows 'I breathe in long'; breathing out long he knows 'I breathe out long'; likewise short in and short out. He trains: 'I shall breathe in (out) experiencing the whole body (sabbakāyapaṭisaṁvedī)'; he trains: 'I shall breathe in (out) calming the bodily formation (passambhayaṁ kāyasaṅkhāraṁ)'. As a skilled turner or turner's apprentice, making a long turn knows 'I make a long turn', and a short turn 'I make a short turn', so the monk knows long and short breaths and trains in the two further steps.
speaker: the Buddha (Bhagavā)

paraphrase: The stated result. In each case the same two fruits may be expected (the text abbreviates the run of durations with …pe…).

paraphrase: Thesis by the six marks. The sutta teaches that the four establishments of mindfulness (contemplating body in body, feelings in feelings, mind in mind, dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending and mindful, without covetousness and displeasure for the world) are the one-way path to purification and nibbāna. Opening and closing (upakrama-upasaṃhāra): the same sentence opens and closes it (mn10:2 and mn10:47), with the theme announced at mn10:3. Repetition (abhyāsa): after each of the twenty-one sections the refrain (internal, external, both; arising and passing away; bare knowledge and recollection; independence; clinging to nothing) recurs, and the whole is closed by the phrase 'thus too he abides contemplating' (mn10:5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 25, 31, 33, 35, 37, 39, 41, 43, 45). Novelty (apūrvatā): the sutta does not itself mark anything as new. Stated result (phala): one of two fruits, final knowledge in this life or non-return if there is a residue, expected within seven years, or seven months, or seven days (mn10:46). Praise (arthavāda): the opening claim (mn10:2, 47) that this is the one-way path for purification, overcoming sorrow, ending pain and realising nibbāna reads as both a doctrinal statement and praise; the sutta gives no further argument for it. Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): none; the sutta instructs and does not argue, apart from the similes (turner, sack of grain, butcher, charnel-ground bodies).
speaker: the Buddha (Bhagavā)
